content: Plate tectonics is the theory that Earth's outer shell (lithosphere) is divided into several plates that glide over the asthenosphereâthe upper part of the mantle. These plates move at rates of 1-15 cm per year, driven primarily by convection currents in the mantle and slab pull (the gravitational force of subducting plates). At plate boundaries, different types of interactions create distinctive geological features. Divergent boundaries occur where plates move apart, creating rift valleys on land and mid-ocean ridges underwater. Magma rises to fill the gap, creating new crust through seafloor spreading. Convergent boundaries form where plates move toward each other. When oceanic crust meets continental crust, the denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate, creating deep ocean trenches, volcanic arcs, and mountain ranges like the Andes. When two continental plates collide, neither subducts; instead, they crumple and thrust upward, forming major mountain ranges like the Himalayas. Transform boundaries occur where plates slide horizontally past each other, creating fault lines prone to earthquakes, such as the San Andreas Fault. The movement of tectonic plates explains continental driftâthe gradual movement of continents over geological time. Evidence for plate tectonics includes the jigsaw-like fit of continents (particularly Africa and South America), similar rock formations and fossil distributions across now-separated continents, paleomagnetism patterns in rocks, and the age distribution of seafloor sediments.

scenario.title: Tectonic Puzzle Explorer
scenario.content: Students manipulate a virtual representation of Earth's lithosphere divided into tectonic plates, controlling their movement over accelerated time scales. The simulation visualizes processes occurring at different depths, from crust through mantle, showing convection currents, magma generation, and crustal deformation. Students can create and observe all three types of plate boundaries (divergent, convergent, transform), watching as distinctive landforms develop at each. The system models realistic physics for earthquake generation, volcanic eruptions, and mountain-building processes. Interactive tools allow students to place markers and measure geological changes over time, create cross-sectional views of subsurface features, and compare current plate configurations with historical arrangements. Challenge scenarios task students with reconstructing past supercontinents or predicting future continental configurations based on current movement vectors.

hypothesis.description: Students will analyze tectonic plate interactions by examining the causes and effects of plate movement. They will predict geological features that form at different boundary types, and explain how these processes shape Earth's surface over geologic time scales.
